utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, can we have the accused or the witness brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can the interpreters hear me? Good morning. Good morning to the Prosecution, the Defence. I am glad to see the accused. You didn't want to come see us, General Blaskic, today? You didn't want to come to the Tribunal, or was it the registry or the detention unit? Who was responsible? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. I think there was a transportation problem, to get from the detention unit to the Tribunal, but I certainly wanted to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's right. I understand. I know you wanted to come. You already came three years ago. But more seriously, what happened, Mr. Registrar? This is the third time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I would like to apologise on behalf of the registry for this delay, and we will make sure that it won't happen again, or in exceptional circumstances only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am a little bit worried by the second part of your sentence, but you're right, try to make your best effort. Will you have enough time, Mr. Nobilo, to finish the examination this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have lost an hour already. I don't think I will be able to finish today, but we are going to take care of most of the final part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that we have now some new figures, Mr. Registrar will confirm them, and I think soon you will be beyond the time that was allocated to you, Mr. Hayman. Mr. Dubuisson, I think you have the figures before you. Can you give them to us? I'm sorry, Mr. Hayman. Maybe we should hear the figures first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There were 60 days allotted to the Defence, and we added 40 minutes after two decisions. The Defence has used 42 days of hearing and 285 minutes; so therefore, the Defence still has this morning seven days of hearings and 35 minutes. As far as the examination-in-chief of the accused Mr. Blaskic is concerned, it lasted 14 days at hearing and 165 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How much did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Fourteen days of hearing and 165 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which means, and I'm referring to the cross-examination, there are still seven days to use by the Prosecution; am I right, Mr. Kehoe? Seven days that you are going to use? And then you will take six days, which will be Defence days but that the Defence doesn't have to give you because the Defence cannot give you any days anymore, and there is another witness that we have to hear too. So the Defence did not fulfil its commitment. But, first of all, Mr. Kehoe, will you be using the same time for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Judge, I have a few questions. I'm not quite sure where that takes us. I suspect I will be using a significant portion of the time, but in all candour and seriousness, Your Honours, it really depends on how the examination goes. With no disrespect to the accused, I'm sure, Mr. President and Your Honour, Judge Shahabuddeen, and Judge -- you didn't have the opportunity to be there at the time, Judge Rodrigues, but nevertheless with Brigadier Marin, the questioning became very difficult because of, in the view of the Prosecutor, I believe non-responsive answers. So it is difficult to gauge, Mr. President, and certainly the Prosecutor has an interest in moving through this as expeditiously as possible. I don't think that -- I'm not sure -- I don't plan on using all that time, but it could very well happen. I didn't plan to do that with Brigadier Marin, but nevertheless, it continued on quite extensively so ... Cross-examination is often a difficult thing to gauge time-wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Hayman, you will have the floor, but the Judges have decided to ask questions to the witness during the proceedings. I think it will shorten the period in which the Judges would have asked questions. But I am still worried. We have a calendar, and in normal circumstances, this calendar should enable us to end by the end of July, if we respect strictly this calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: I think that if the Prosecution was to use the same time during the cross-examination as the Defence in the examination-in-chief of General Blaskic as a witness and given the calendar of the Judges and the availability of the courtroom, it would be almost impossible to finish by the end of July, and I think this would be very difficult for the parties and for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know that a trial is made up of various actors acting in contradiction with each other, and the Judges are there to synthesise the proceedings, but we have to acknowledge that if we don't finish this trial by the 13th (sic) of July -- let me remind you that it was supposed to finish by the end of June and then the end of July -- if we don't finish this trial by the end of July, I don't know where we're going to go. We will have to start the trial again at the beginning of September, and you know that it will be, in September, 25 months of trial, and in my personal capacity, I would say that it's too much, but I want it to be said in the transcript that it is my personal opinion, but still I think it is too long. If we observe other trials in the area of international law, in Nuremberg and Tokyo, I have to admit that there is something wrong. Twenty-five months; there is something wrong with the procedure, and maybe the Judges are partly responsible for it, but there we have to think about it. But the main problem is to try and finish the trial by the 31st of July. The Defence used more time, but how can we solve the problem? Of course, the rights of the accused have to be respected. I think, Mr. Hayman, that there is another witness you want to call. Normally we should forbid this. So what's your opinion? What do you think? How can we finish the trial by the end of July? Is the burden going to end on the Prosecution side? This is not a closed session. I want the public gallery to hear this debate. Twenty-five months of trial for General Blaskic. Why not 26? Why not 32? There is something wrong. It goes beyond reason. Mr. Hayman, you chose the statements and the testimony of Mr. Blaskic. That was your choice. So my question is: How can we finish by the 31st of July? The Judges have very busy schedules. I don't even know what Judge Shahabuddeen is going to do because he is a member of the Appeals Chamber, he is the Vice-President of the Tribunal, Judge Rodrigues had to read 18.000 pages of transcript to take over after Judge Riad, and the Judges cannot work any more. We will have to make a decision on this. In other Chambers, for instance, the Judges use four or five months to render a judgment when they had shorter trials. I don't know. I don't know how we can finish. Mr. Hayman, what happened? You usually respect the Trial Chamber's decision, so what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, first of all, I would say to the Court, it was the Defence that advocated time limits in this case, it was the Defence that asked that a limit be placed on the Prosecutor, and it was the Defence that offered to have an imbalance in the length of the respective cases of the parties in this case, and we offered to voluntarily give up approximately a third of the time that we would otherwise have if we were to have an equivalent period of time as the Prosecutor. We offered to use only 60 days in our case as opposed to, I believe, 90 or more days which were actually used by the Prosecutor in his case in chief. So we have been a proponent of focused, efficient efforts and time limits; and I would say, on that score, the Court is in a good position to evaluate whether the Defence, particularly as compared to the Prosecutor, have we brought direct evidence relevant to the charges in this case, documents that are directly relevant, testimony that is directly relevant, as opposed to the year of "circumstantial," quote, unquote, "victim," quote, unquote, testimony that we were all forced to listen to by the Prosecutor with virtually no, if not no, direct evidence bearing on the charges. So I submit to you that the Defence has done an outstanding job of bringing to the Court pointed material, relevant evidence, and trying very hard to move our case along and present witnesses in as short a time period as possible. I agree, the testimony of the accused has gone on for some time, and I will address that. We, Mr. Nobilo and I and the accused, we formed a plan, a strategy, for our case, with the goal of completing our case in 60 days, and I think we have come darn close, we have come very close to that goal, and I congratulate my fellow members of the Defence team for doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But before congratulating each other, I think you have a way of reversing the situation which was quite comical. I am a bit dramatic. I know you're a very clever lawyer, but we have a public hearing today. I am talking about the discontent of the Judges because you went beyond the time allocated to the Defence. And what do I hear? You congratulate each other for what happened. I don't agree. I don't agree. The commitments were set by the Chamber on your proposal, so you can't say now, "Well, we had set a period of 60 days. We could have asked for more." I think this is a sophism. "I asked for 60 days and now I'm talking 90 days so I'm right and I would like to congratulate myself." No, you can't really follow that reasoning. I can't admit this. You had said 60 days you had to respect this time limit, and this was the time the Trial Chamber made a decision on. So now we can't say, "We could have used 90 days, we could have used 120 days." Maybe the Trial Chamber wouldn't have agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I didn't say, Mr. President, that we should have used 90 days or 120 days or that we intend to. Please, please, do not attribute words to me that I haven't said. What I said is, we formed a reasonable plan to complete our case within the time period allotted by the Court, and we began the testimony of the accused, who we believed to be the last witness in the case, not counting yesterday's witness, and we started the testimony of the accused with -- well, let's count back -- with 21 or 22 days remaining of the Defence's time. Was that a reasonable plan on the part of the Defence, to leave 21 or 22 full trial day equivalents which, in this court, is over two months of sitting, of calendar time, was it reasonable for us to leave that period of time within which to conclude the Defence's case, or should the Defence have allotted 50 per cent, not just approximately 40 per cent of its time, for the testimony of the accused, should we have allotted 50 per cent of our apportioned time for the testimony of the accused? I think we've acted reasonably. I think the length of the testimony of the accused has been somewhat unpredictable. It has been lengthened by the extensive questioning of the Court which we welcome and think is efficient and will promote an efficient and timely conclusion to the case, but that is an unpredictable element, and I submit that the Court's questioning has comprised perhaps 10 or 13 per cent of the total direct examination. The defence is not accusing anyone of doing anything wrong, but I would ask the Court, please, to accept the fact that the Defence in good faith has worked very hard to stay within the budgeted time that the Court gave us and that we the Defence, in fact, asked to be imposed on us. The question you posed, Mr. President, how do we finish in July, because we must, and the Defence agrees we must finish this case reasonably soon and certainly by July. We are all fatigued mentally and physically. The case has gone on for years, and we must bring it to a resolution. We have several suggestions. We are eager to work full days on any days that the Court and the courtroom are available. We agree with that suggestion. If there are periods of time when all three of Your Honours are not available, I believe the Defence can agree to proceed by Rule 71 procedures so that we do not lose weeks during breaks, because if we lose two weeks, a month, in some of these remaining months, it may well be impossible, as the Court's legal advisor indicates, to finish by July. We also have a related concern, and that is if the cross-examination of the accused stretches out over six weeks or even seven weeks, we think that's unfair because then the cross-examination also becomes some kind of a strange memory quiz where testimony is so prolonged and elongated, and there undoubtedly will be references to earlier testimony, direct, cross-examination, et cetera. It becomes difficult for any witness, and there is an added layer of difficulty which we think is objectionable. We would urge the Court to use as much of every available day so that the cross-examination in terms of calendar days can be compressed into a reasonable period of time. We have, over the several days and earlier, been trying to eliminate portions of the direct examination to further condense the remaining material we have. Most of the remaining material, Mr. President and Your Honours, consists of confrontation, where the witness will directly confront testimony of other witnesses that have been given. We'll put the transcripts of that other testimony on the ELMO, and the witness will directly comment and respond to it. It's very important testimony. We can't eliminate it. Although we must and we urge the Court to try and compress the proceedings from here on in, as we have been urging, the testimony of the accused is the wrong place, we think, to apply a surgical knife, and we would urge the Court not to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I commend your goodwill, Mr. Hayman. Of course, you understood that when I said "90 days," that it was just a figure, although I think that if we add one-third to 60 days, we should be around 90 days. I think it's a little bit easy for you to say, "Now we have to act expeditiously. Now we have to condense. Now we have to make efforts," and, of course, this is funny to realise that now we're going to start with the cross-examination of the witness, now we're going to hear court witnesses one day each, but if the Judges were going to use the same method as you, it wouldn't be possible, given the nature of the witnesses called by the Judges. If we compare, for instance, General Morillon's Brigadier Marin, we would need at least two months to hear General Morillon. So I don't think your position is good as a principle, your position which is "Let's make some efforts now," and it's funny to realise that now. It's the Prosecution who's going to ask questions to the accused and the Judges. You have one witness left. Are you going to call this witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We will have to make suitable security arrangements in consultation with the host country if that witness is to come and testify. That is a matter we will raise with the Court in writing on Monday, I expect, and depending on whether those security arrangements are possible, the witness either will or will not be able to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The third point before we start our proceedings again, but it's not a waste of time, I can assure you. This is a great concern for the Judges. If there is an unavailability of one of the Judges, can Article 71 apply? I shall turn to the Prosecution for this. Let me remind you that our Rule 71 will be applied at this stage of the trial only if the Defence, the accused, and the Prosecution agree. In other circumstances, it will not be applied. We will ask for the agreement of the three parties. Now I shall turn to the Prosecution for an answer, maybe not today. Don't give it today if you don't have it today, but I would like to remind you that everybody will have to agree on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I'd like to say that we don't have an answer at this point on that proposition. I would like to make some comments in respect of my colleague's comments. I appreciate Your Honours' observations in respect of the time. Even though Mr. Hayman accuses the Prosecutor, once again, of being at fault for the length of this trial, I think the facts will speak for themselves. In respect of Mr. Hayman's comments as to the Prosecutor's evidence and the quality of the evidence that the Prosecutor presented during her case in chief, Mr. President, that's appropriate for final argument and not for comment at this point in time. I repeat what my colleague said. He proposed the time limits. It was not the Prosecutor that proposed those, but we accepted the decision of the Court and the proposal of counsel. He set 60 days as his time limit. We met a 90-day time limit, and in the process of that, we did not call certain witnesses we intended to call. We respected the Court's decision. We respected the time limit. We calculated accordingly, and we have met our obligations under the decision of this Court. The Defence is the master of its own destiny. They suggested 60 days. It was the Defence that suggested a time frame that they said they would meet. In fact, they said they anticipated at one point being short of 60 days. Now, obviously strategies change, and I accept that. Nevertheless, it was the Defence that decided to put Colonel Blaskic on the stand for 13 days to testify at length about many matters that were not relevant in this particular hearing. Mr. President, the Prosecutor would urge this Court to respect the orders that it has made, to respect the obligations that had been suggested be imposed by counsel that the Prosecutor met, and respect the time limit. In our calculation, Mr. President, the cross-examination, there are seven and a half days left or seven days and 35 minutes left. I think it's reasonable to anticipate that the cross-examination may well take all of that time, in which case, in our view, the Defence time has been extinguished. It's over. In our view, Mr. President, at the end of the cross-examination of Colonel Blaskic, the Defence case is finished, and the calling of an additional witness, as they did yesterday, out of order essentially was a way of expanding their witness list. Calling a witness after the cross-examination is a way of again expanding beyond the time frame they said they would meet and which this Court ordered. Now, I have to say, Mr. President, I'm absolutely astonished at the change in position that the Defence has tendered to this Court that it is now acceptable to proceed by Rule 71 deposition in the cross-examination of Colonel Blaskic when it wasn't acceptable in the direct examination of Colonel Blaskic. That reluctance to accept Rule 71 deposition testimony on the direct examination certainly slowed down these proceedings. It resulted in the change of the bench of this Trial Chamber, but now what was not okay on direct examination apparently is okay on cross-examination. We will reserve, Mr. President, our views, and we will certainly give them in respect of the Rule 71 deposition, but that is a shift in situation that, to me, is astonishing. Now, I have a suggestion, Mr. President, because we would like to end this as well, and I think there is consensus, even with my colleagues across the way, we would like to end this case by July, but one suggestion I have is this: The Court is going to engage in hearing additional witnesses in respect of sentencing, and our view is that it would be one very good area where Rule 71 depositions could take place, that we could finish the trial of this case, and in respect of the witnesses who will be testifying for sentencing, we could present the depositions of those testimonies to this Trial Chamber, the depositions and the videos. That's one possibility. We certainly urge this Court at any opportunity that arises, if there's a cancellation in other court hearings to fill -- those voids created by unforeseen events in other court proceedings, to fill it with this trial. We would accept that. We also accept the idea of on any given day where we can proceed on full days now through July 31st, that we will accept that as well. Those are the views of the Prosecutor, Mr. President and Your Honours. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to present them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you of our order -- I don't see the date -- of the 17th of December. The Prosecutor will have 39 days; the Defence will have 60 days of hearings. We ask the registrar to keep track of the days used. It is up to the parties to submit serious arguments for any extension of these delays and that they will be granted only exceptionally. I would like to ask Mr. Hayman whether he considers that within the frame work of this last paragraph of this order to present serious arguments in favour of his motion because this is an order issued in December 1997, and it says that it is up to the parties to submit serious arguments in support of any motions to extend the time and that such motions would be granted only exceptionally. I do not wish to choose any other strategy except the one you yourself have proposed. If you wish to go beyond the conditions of this order, you have to present very serious arguments in favour. Also, I ask the Prosecution to consider the provisions of Rule 71, as well as the accused, because only under exceptional circumstances can this apply. If we can gain one day, we will do so, but I don't see much possibility for doing so. I think we will be keeping the closing arguments as short as possible, and as from now on, the Rules of Procedure will be applied fully and, of course, equally to those parties. Those Rules allow the President and the Chamber -- let me repeat what I was saying. I asked the Defence to bear in mind that the time has expired allotted to the Defence. Have you managed to translate that? Yes? Therefore, the Defence has used its time. Also, in accordance with the order of December 1997, if the Defence has any serious arguments to present a last witness, it should present them. Thirdly, regarding the application of Rule 71, which is applied only exceptionally, the Chamber will require the unanimous agreement of both parties and the accused. Fourthly, I asked the Prosecution to bear in mind that its cross-examination is fixed within the same time period as the examination-in-chief, and if there is any way of gaining time, that it do so. I also asked both the Defence and the Prosecution to tell us how much time will be needed for sentencing and the time needed for the closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm happy to address those, Mr. President. First of all, I have a suggestion that I think could save us a week of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's a decision, Mr. Hayman, but you may make a comment. You said that you could answer. You may only make a comment, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can always only make a comment, Mr. President, of course. I understand that. My suggestion on saving time is this: The Rules provide for the filing of the final brief one week before closing argument. In this case, given the size and duration of the case, the final briefs of the parties will be hundreds of pages in length, perhaps 300, 400, or even 500 pages each. They obviously will not be translated before closing argument for Your Honour, and, indeed, it will be difficult for even the English speaking member or members of the Trial Chamber to review the final briefs, yet this requirement will necessitate at least an extra week break, such that the evidence would have to conclude, say, on day 1, the final brief could be due on day 7, and then final arguments could commence seven days later on day 14. That's how, under the current Rules, the end of the case would have to occur. If the Court allows the final briefs to be filed after final argument, 7 or 10 or 14 days after final argument, I think one week of the break can be eliminated, so the final argument could take seven days after the conclusion of the evidence, not 14 days. Because if that final brief has to be filed seven days before final argument, it would be impossible, I think, for the parties to finish the evidence on day 1, file an intelligent final brief of 500 pages in length on day 1, and then be prepared for closing argument on day 7. So I make that humble suggestion for the Court's consideration. In terms of sentencing evidence, the Defence expects three calendar days, at the most, of sentencing material. That's our current estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Fourmy, 14 days or five days for the final brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: The Rules envisage five days between the submission of the final brief and the closing argument. I think that 14 days is envisaged if the final brief is submitted on a Friday; then on the following week, on Monday, the closing arguments can be presented. The point is that the written document could be submitted after the final arguments, so we would gain some time in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges will consider carefully your proposals, Mr. Hayman. Any further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to closing argument, keeping in mind the need for speed and a timely conclusion of the case, we think it would be unrealistic to allocate less than one week for closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One week for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One week total, Mr. President, and that's an estimate, but we don't think closing argument can be concluded in one or two days. We are waiting to hear if closing argument will consist of one argument on each side, that is, by each party, or whether we will proceed, as the Rules, envision with four arguments. We think argument could be shorter if there are two arguments, but the Rules provide for four, and we are waiting for further guidance from the Court on that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. As there are no further comments for the time being, we can continue. Judge Rodrigues, would you like to intervene? Judge Shahabuddeen? No? Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, may we return to presenting the final chronology? Could you tell us, up to the end of January, in fact, when was the guards unit finally set up and in what way were the special purposes units abolished finally?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the orders of the 15th of January, 1993, unleashed a process of the formation of the 3rd Guards Brigade, and sometime at the end of January already, we had a review of those portions of the command and units which we had succeeded in forming up until then, and, at the same time, from the 15th of January onwards, in legal terms, the process began to abolish the special purposes units, the Vitezovi and the light assault battalion. Of course, this process lasted, in the period to come, it lasted in February and went on to March. But from the 15th of January, 1993, the order was issued, and I issued it, for the formation of the 3rd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you receive the order appointing you to another duty, that is to say, formally speaking, when did you cease being the commander of the Vitez military district?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received the order on the 26th of April, perhaps it was the 27th or 28th of April, but it was thereabouts, 1994, that is, that I had been appointed to perform the duty of deputy chief of the main staff of the HVO and that I was promoted to the rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally asked the chief of the main staff to permit me to remain in Vitez in the Central Bosnia operative command until the first half of May, 1994. It was until about the 13th or the 15th of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you receive your new orders and promotion?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I was appointed to the following tasks and assignments on the 6th of August, 1994, and I took up my duties as chief of the main staff of the HVO, and in August, I don't remember the exact date, but I became the commander of the joint command of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was one of the commanders, and the other commander was General Rasim Delic who, at the same time, was the commander of the staff of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us return to your first promotion. Tell us what the political circumstances were and the practical circumstances which led to your promotion, first of all, when you became deputy chief of staff, that is in 1994, and your appointment as Major-General?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The date, I said the 26th of April, 1994. So what were the circumstances which led to your promotion from the 26th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall have to go back in time several days. Sometime around the 25th of February, 1994, an agreement was signed for a cease-fire between the HVO units and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and sometime in the first half of March, I know that the Washington Agreement was signed by which the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed, and the president of the federation, as far as I recall, was Mr. Kresimir Zubak, and the vice-president of the federation was Mr. Ejup Ganic. I know that the president up until then of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, before the Washington Agreement, had tendered his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name was Mr. Mate Boban. And that his state functions, so to speak, were taken over by Mr. Kresimir Zubak. After the signing of the Washington Agreement, and this was sometime at the beginning of April 1994, from the main staff, for the first time, an inspection, the main inspection arrived of the Croatian Defence Council, and for a period of 15 to 20 days, it undertook a complete inspection of the Lasva pocket and the areas of Kiseljak, around Kiseljak, and the Zepce area. After carrying out this principal inspection, also in the first half of April 1994, the Lasva pocket was visited by the president of the federation, Mr. Kresimir Zubak, and he talked with me, had a conversation with me, and asked me to give him a brief about the military situation; and while parts of the inspection team were still in Kiseljak, I was with the inspection team in the second half of April, and that is where I was faxed information that I had been appointed deputy chief of the main staff of the HVO and that I had been promoted to the rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, at that time, when decisions were being made concerning your promotion, did you talk to the new president, Mr. Zubak, and if you did, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I -- that is to say, President Zubak, Mr. Kresimir Zubak, had a lengthy conversation with me in Vitez, and he told me that one of the basic tasks of the creation and building up of the army of the federation, that that was a basic task, and that his criterion was professionalism and honesty of the cadres and personnel, that in selecting cadres and personnel, he would be guided by the personnel in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The federation consisted of which parties? Would you remind us of that? The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was its relationship in relation to the former HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know the area and the borders at that time, and I don't even think they were defined as such, but the federation consisted, if we look at the surface area, of the components of the BH army and components of the HVO, the military components, and the area which was controlled by those two military forces became part of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is a kind of Croato-Muslim federation in preparation, isn't it, in relation to what will be done at Dayton?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. It was the Washington Agreement which led to the formation of the Croato-Muslim federation and the signing of the draft or programme of the organisation of the federation and its constitution and the constitution of the federal army of the federation which was proposed of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council. So it had two components, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, in a situation when you received your promotion and when a new politician came to lead the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Zubak, what did you understand by this? What decision was made with regard to Herceg-Bosna? What happened to Herceg-Bosna at that particular moment in time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the president, Mr. Zubak, told me that it was the beginning of the building up of the federation and that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was being ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So your promotion came when the decision was made to, so to speak, abolish Herceg-Bosna, but tell us, as a military man, from this distance in time, if you can compare Kresimir Zubak and Mate Boban as politicians, as two politicians, which of these two men was more moderate? Which one was more an extremist Croat politician? Who was more cooperative towards the Muslims? Could you tell us this with the hindsight that you have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, at all events, Mr. Kresimir Zubak was, in cadres terms, acceptable, an acceptable choice for building up the federation, both by the representatives of the International Community and, as far as I know, and he told me this himself, that the strategy was to move resolutely towards building up a federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is what he emphasised frequently, on many occasions. I was not personally included into the political structures for me to be able to make an assessment of the concrete qualities of each man as a politician, but the very choice and options for new cadres showed that these were the options of most of the political representatives, the Croats, because what Mate Boban put forward was accepted at a broader political meeting which I did not attend and I only know what others informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From this distance, how do you assess the decision that a new politician, who has the task of building up a joint state with the Muslims, appointed precisely you later on for the first soldier of the Croatian side? How do you assess that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I believe that he kept to his principle and that he selected those cadres who would be able to build up the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, with the application of the Washington Agreement later, Dayton, in which segment was there cooperation first and best between the Croats and the Muslims in that BH federation?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Excuse me. I am sorry for interrupting the examination, but it seems to me that I have a problem. It says in English here that there was a meeting "... because what Mate Boban put forward was accepted at a broader political meeting which I did not attend and I only know what others informed me." I wonder whether the Mate Boban that General Blaskic referred to, I have a feeling that he was referring to Mr. Zubak. I am not quite sure whether Defence can check the transcript to see whether an error has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which line is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: 1354, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps the parties can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I don't think that we can put this back on our monitor, but we can ask General Blaskic once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it a meeting in Livno? Were you talking about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but I said that a little earlier on. Your Honours, I said that there was a meeting in Livno of politicians of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and at that meeting, Mr. Mate Boban resigned, tendered his resignation, and at that meeting, the new official, Mr. Kresimir Zubak, was appointed, promoted. But I was not present at that meeting and I only have knowledge that I heard from others, and President Zubak told me of that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should now like to pass around two documents at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit number D553 and D554; 554 is the document of Mostar, 6th of May, '94, and the other one is 553.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Both these documents are dated the 6th of May, but one refers to the appointment, that is to say, deputy chief of the main staff, and the second is the rank. Perhaps we could define the two documents in that way? So what number does the document concerning rank, Major-General, have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, are these the documents concerning your appointment that you mentioned, the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Kresimir Zubak, and the promotion document where you were promoted to Major-General, also signed by Kresimir Zubak, are those the two documents in question?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but the document with regard to my appointment, the date there, when I took up my duties, it says the 26th of April, 1994, and around about the end of April, I was informed of this document regarding the appointment, and the 6th of May document is the document which refers to my promotion to the rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, Mr. Zubak, he is what? I understood that he was president of the federation, and here it says he is president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, he was the president of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, at the same time, president of the presidential council of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were appointed General but only for the Croatian part of the army. I'm afraid I don't understand very well.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this phase, that is to say, in May 1994, I was appointed to the duty of deputy chief of the main staff of the HVO only for that part of the HVO, whereas in August 1994, I got my next promotion where I was appointed to two duties: the chief of the main staff of the HVO and, at the same time, the commander in this command of the army of the federation for the HVO component of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the transition period, the army of the federation did keep both components: the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO? Is that the way it was regulated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's the way it was regulated, and Mr. Rasim Delic and I, with our associates, we were only supposed to embark upon the creation of the army of the federation, that is to say, setting up the military component and seeing to the establishment of the Ministries of Defence of the armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. In August, you still remained in the HVO section?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, until the 14th of August, approximately, I was head of the main staff of the HVO, and on the 14th of August, a meeting was held that I attended and also Mr. Kresimir Zubak; the Minister of Defence of the federation, Mr. Jadranko Prlic; and then the president of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic; then the commander of the staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Rasim Delic; then the president of the government, the prime minister of the federation, Mr. Haris Silajdzic; and then it was decided at that meeting that I and Mr. Rasim Delic should be commanders of that command of the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, to follow the President's question, after that meeting was held and you were appointed joint commander of the army of the federation, did you continue to occupy a military position in relation to the army of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, because this was envisaged by the Washington Accords. Both I and Rasim Delic ex officio checked our positions in our respective armies, he in the BH army, I in the HVO, but at the same time, we were in charge of building the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see, General. It's clear to me now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, that, indeed, helps us to understand, so in the federation, each one will retain his respective role, whereas at the same time, the two commanders in chief are entrusted with establishing the future army. That is, I think, clear now, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, when you were in that meeting and there was Izetbegovic and there were other officers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and top politicians of the Muslim side, did anybody have any objections and did anybody try to stop your appointment to the joint command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No one tried to stop it, as far as I remember. Aside from Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, and Mr. Delic, I think that Mr. Ejup Ganic was also there, but I know that not then or not later did this happen, because I had quite a few meetings afterwards with Mr. Rasim Delic in terms of developing the army of the federation and also in terms of carrying out joint actions that we did carry out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As we were liberating these territories, nobody ever made any objections to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any problems in the cooperation with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was there any animosity on the side of the junior officers in the joint actions that you carried out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never noticed any such problems, and, indeed, I had quite a bit of contact. Practically every week, there was a minimum of one contact per week. We also elaborated joint plans and we held meetings, and there was coordination on the ground. I personally travelled to Sarajevo frequently as well as to other areas under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At checkpoints, it was the military police of the BH army that stopped me, there were junior officers and senior officers, and there was never any animosity whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Except for you and President Zubak, after the Washington Accords were signed and the decision was reached to build a state and army together with the Muslims, were there any changes in terms of the other posts, for example, the Ministry of Defence and other key ministries?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were changes. I know for sure there were in the Ministry of Defence. A new minister of defence came approximately at that time. Then there were also changes in the army. I'm far more familiar with the cadre changes that took place then, and the operational zone commanders were changed, such as the operational zone of Mostar's commander, and there were quite a few other cadre changes. Also, appointments were to be made in the joint headquarters of the new army in Sarajevo. There were new officers that were supposed to come in, and we were also building this infrastructure because this was the very beginning of the building of the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At this point in time, now that we're almost over, if we are to look at your entire service in Bosnia in the HVO, could you tell us, what is the main characteristic of the posts you held, and how did you envisage your basic role in 1992? What was it like in the beginning of 1993 in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia and what was it like from April 1993 onwards, in a sentence or two?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I came to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the invitation of the president of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak with the main objective of organising defence from aggression by the army of Republika Srpska, and I spent most of my time at the front line in Kiseljak, and after that in Jajce, Travnik. These were front lines vis-a-vis the army of Republika Srpska. At that time, there was practically not a single position that I did not come to and where I did not spend some time. At the end of 1992, we managed, through a concerted effort, to stabilise the front line in Travnik, and after this first joint command was set up, I primarily made efforts to organise the HVO from the ranks of the armed people and these peasants, and I tried to turn them into a military organisation. From the 16th of April, 1993, my fundamental task was to survive and to have these pockets survive because I was aware that if any one of the pockets were to fall, it is certain that we would have disappeared altogether from the territory of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The war with the Muslims, did you plan that? Did anybody order you about that, and did you have any idea when you came to Bosnia that you would be waging war against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never planned this war with the Muslims, and I claim, with full responsibility, that not a single one of my associates in the command of the Operative Zone ever took part in the elaboration of any plan concerning warfare with the Muslims. From the first time I came to Kiseljak, I always believed that we had to act together against a common enemy. At that time, it was the army of Republika Srpska. I made every effort to have this joint command work, and wherever I was, either in Jajce or in Maglaj or Olovo, I helped the joint defence and the efforts to survive at these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anybody ever ask you to do this, and did you ever order the use of troops in the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from the area of the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No one ever asked me to do that, and even had anyone asked me to do it, I never would have carried out such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, we saw that you were in a difficult situation, major tasks and no organisation whatsoever. In that desperate situation for you personally, why did you not resign and, in this way, avoid everything that happened to you subsequently and avoid the trial that is still going on? Why didn't you say, "I've had enough. I'm going home to Austria"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Had it been any other job or any amount of money, there is no money that could be paid for that kind of work. This was not a job. I took this as my duty, my obligation, and a matter of conscience. I was supposed to help. I remained when I found out that Buhine Kuce had fallen and that one pocket was turned into two. In January 1994, I was in Austria, but I knew that this was a sinking ship, and my conscience would not have allowed me to abandon ship. I had highlighted that Bosnia-Herzegovina was my homeland too, and it was my obligation to give my contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned a job. In 1992 and in 1993, as the commander of the Operative Zone, how much money did you make?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not make any money, nor did we, in 1992 and 1993, at least in my command, have any kind of earnings, except for food parcels that were distributed to those members of the command who were at the very brink of existence. We did not have a budget at all anyway because, for the most part, it was the municipalities that had financed the home guard units, and only the military police and the special purpose units received financing from the department of defence or, rather, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Finally, when you became chief of the main staff of the HVO, what was your attitude towards the authorities, civilian or military, of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never received any order from the head of the main staff of the Croatian army, nor any instructions, nor any orders from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, nor did I ever send any reports to those institutions. I sent regular reports to the minister of defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the minister of defence of the federation and the president of the presidential council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: While you were in the Lasva Valley, did you ever get any orders from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never got any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you hear of your indictment here before this Court in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember the event but I do not recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Approximately what time of the year was it and which year was this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was the beginning of November 1995. On the next day, I was supposed to meet with General Walker in Sarajevo and with General Delic, and late in the evening, I left the main staff and was travelling towards Citluk where I was staying. My wife informed me en route that she had heard on the HTV news that this had been broadcast. Then I made a phone call to Sarajevo, and I asked whether there would be a meeting. I made a phone call to the joint command. I didn't know what to do. I was told that the meeting that was supposed to be held was to be postponed, that it would not be held that morning; otherwise I was supposed to leave at 3.00 in the morning so that I could reach Sarajevo on time, as I was leaving from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You and your wife, where were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the house of Danko Dugandzic. It was really an adapted garage, a ground floor, two-room apartment, and one was very damp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You did not own it. You had rented it; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was the property of Mr. Danko Dugandzic, quite modest, and it was rented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened then? When did you decide to surrender, and what action did you take in that direction?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, before that decision, while these Dayton talks were still on, I was appointed inspector in the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian army. I was appointed to that post, although there were no consultations that were held with me. At that time, I was not consulted with this appointment at all, and I found out about this appointment via Croatian television. It had been broadcast. After that, also at the end of November, I had to travel to Zagreb, since my wife was pregnant. She had quite a few problems with this pregnancy, and she had to be examined by specialists. I visited the family of General Binenfeld from Zagreb, and I talked to him and his wife about this situation, and already then I told him that I would come here to The Hague. He supported this idea, and he said that that was the right choice to make and that I was supposed to take my passport, to pack my things, and to go to The Hague. His son was also present there. His name is Jasa Binenfeld.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, at that time, did Croatia have any legal possibility of extraditing you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, as I am not a legal person, there was no legal possibility to do so because this law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal had not been passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did the constitution regulate the extradition of Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying, to the best of my knowledge, it was not possible, according to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, to extradite Croatian citizens to the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the interpreters have been working for the past hour and twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I was thinking of the break, primarily for the interpreters. I just wanted to know whether you have some more general questions and how much more time will you need with the accused. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, by all means, we're going to use all the remaining time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a 20-minute break then and resume work at 11.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May I have Prosecution document 456/49?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution document. And document 456/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, these are two documents, Prosecution documents. Look at them carefully. They are your orders dated the 19th of April, both orders are dated the 19th of April, but the first order was written at 18.45 and the second 21.40, sent to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, and it concerns an order for attack with regard to the Gomionica village. Would you read the two documents, please? We're not going to read through them all together. Have you read them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, what you ordered. Was it an attack on the village, civilians, or what?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in point 3 of the order, I ordered that attacks be launched in groups and only diagonally from the positions of Kocatale and from the position of Sikulja. That area which I ordered to be attacked is an area which is well-known to me. I personally toured it, and I know that that is where the military positions of the BH army were located. I visited the area in a previous period. It was sometime between February and March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Had the attack been launched according to your order of the 19th of April at 18.45, point 3, would the HVO have entered the village or would it have gone around the village of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The HVO would have gone around the village, circumvented the village, because the village of Gomionica was not the assignment of the HVO, it was the hill above Gomionica, and perhaps the best thing would be for me to point it out on the model once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have already pointed this out to us once, the plan of attack, but briefly, please, indicate the axes of attack according to your order.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, point 3 of my order required that the attack be launched from the positions of Kocatale diagonally, that is to say, up on the hill towards this position here (indicating), and from Sikulje towards this position here (indicating) on the combat groups, that is to say, the smaller parts which the commanders would be able to control fully. On the map, the positions at Kocatale -- I am pointing to that position now -- and the Sikulje position, so part of the force of the attack was to go from Sikulje towards this diagonal line and for the other line from Kocatale towards feature 759.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, Kiseljak, where were the command posts and the bulk of the BH army forces?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The command post was in Gomionica and most of the bulk of the forces were also in Gomionica, but they were deployed along the hills above the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us whether, according to the knowledge you have now, after this procedure, whether the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade acted according to your orders or did it launch the attack in another way?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It did not follow my orders. The attack was conducted frontally, from the main road towards the village of Gomionica and in the direction of the hill, but later on, they did follow my orders. Unfortunately, a little more time elapsed before this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is Defence document D335.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Document 335 is your note or your report from a meeting with the BH army. Can you tell us a few words about how the document came into being?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wrote the document and it is a report from a meeting that was held on the 21st of April, 1993, and here it states there were representatives of the BH army and it was chaired by Mr. Thebault, and I always wrote documents in a complete fashion and I stated what each of the participants at the meeting said and what I myself said at the meeting in question, and I always endeavoured to record everything as exactly as possible, that is to say, everything that those present at the meeting discussed and said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at that particular meeting which was attended by the most responsible representatives of the 3rd Corps and the BH army, did anybody mention at all the suffering of the civilians and the crime in Ahmici, and the meeting was held on the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, nobody mentioned the crime in Ahmici, but there was mention, not at the meeting but from what I was able to note, that there were a large number of civilian casualties, but it was an assertion without any specifics. Nobody specified the positions to which this might refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you make a note of that assertion and did you send it to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wrote down everything that I heard at the meeting, that I heard discussed at the meeting, during the official part of the meeting and the free discussions that took place in the break of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The title "Other Observations," in point 6, you state as follows: "Merdan finds some simple causes to the conflict. He is fairly worried because of the 500 killed civilians in Vitez."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or words to that effect. We haven't got the document, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, first of all, what "Other Observations" refers to and what the difference is between "Other Observations" and previous contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the contents of the document, I list everything that was discussed at the official part of the meeting, and I always wrote in the first person singular and I would write the name and surname in the margin beside and then what that person said, I would write this in the first person singular, and "Other Observations" are my observations, that is to say, what I heard on the spot as was said, as I heard it from people at that time. So it wasn't the contents of the official discussion held at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From the circumstances, that is to say, that at the official part of the meeting, nobody mentioned the civilian casualties and that Dzemo Merdan just mentioned in passing a large number of civilians, 500, in fact, that were killed. What were you able to deduce, to conclude, from that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I considered that that figure was unrealistic and that quite possibly this was being used as a negotiating tactic at that particular moment, all the more so as it was the position both of General Halilovic and General Petkovic that it was urgently needed to tour the Busovaca front line, to go to that line; in concrete terms, the position at Kula. And that is where they went. They went to visit that position at Kula on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We can go on now to Prosecution Exhibit 456/58.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at the document, please. It is your report, it is a Prosecution Exhibit dated the 24th of April, 1993, sent to the vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, head of the defence department, and the chief of the main staff of the HVO, and you are informing them about the discussion with Colonel Stewart, commander of the English United Nations battalion, the talk that was held the same day with Stewart and linked to the suffering --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, with all due respect. Mr. President, we have done this already, as we have with the prior document. Have we not discussed this document in earnest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I am a little disturbed, Mr. Nobilo, if we're going to go through all the documents that we have already seen with the accused. I don't know what your aim is. I cannot prevent you in developing your strategy. But I must say that I am rather disturbed if we are going to talk about Gomionica, Kuber. I really don't understand what the purpose is. To show him the document that the accused himself had issued? The Judges have seen those documents. What is your aim?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We thought in this part that we should confront the witness with all potentially -- I am saying "potentially" -- troublesome documents or statements, and we shall only go through a few documents and we shall dwell, for the longest period, on the statements that were not dealt with until now at all. We wanted General Blaskic to say something about some of the documents that the Prosecutor showed to every witness who came to this court. But if you believe that this has sufficiently been clarified in the previous period, then we can confront him with the statements made by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know how attentive the Judges are of the rights of the accused, but I am asking myself -- you had six weeks to organise your strategy. If today, in two hours, we have to finish, and if, on the last day, you want to show the accused all the documents, I will have to consult with my colleagues, if you are going to show him all the statements, explanations. The accused has had six weeks to answer your questions, and I am a bit disturbed. I am not saying that you can't do it. But how long will all this take?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For these documents, we will need very little time, as you saw in the case of this document; namely, the witness presented the events chronologically, and many things are, in a certain way, lost in a chronology. We found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That was your choice, Mr. Nobilo, the presentation of the chronology. Let me remind you of this. Please wait a moment, Mr. Hayman. Let me finish. We had this discussion, I'm sure you remember it, regarding that chronology. I am going to slow down. You said that "We have chosen this chronological presentation from the beginning of the conflict until the promotion of the accused to General-Inspector of the Croatian army." You chose this strategy. You could have started with this, for instance. And the Judges respected your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have believed and do believe that we made the right choice. The presentation was chronological and there was a certain logic to that, but finally, we thought that it was necessary to deal with certain subject-related areas, and that will not take too much time, and since we are talking about two years of war pregnant with events, we thought that this was the best way to deal with it: chronologically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but if, for two years of war, the trial of the accused has to last two years, it is not a question of the duration of the war. If we need two years for the Defence for two years of war, I must remind you that you have already exhausted your time. Let me consult with my colleagues. Just a moment. Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. Yes, I promised to give you the floor. Please, let's hear your remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to add, to speed the chronology, we omitted showing the witness many documents so we could go through the chronology and give the Court that picture. Had we dealt with all of the documents during the chronology, the chronology would have been even longer. There are certain important documents. We think it's significant for the witness to look at and directly comment on the documents, and that's what we seek to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- on that last issue raised by Mr. Hayman, what matters is this particular document went on for hours and hours, and I direct Your Honour to the meeting that the accused had with Colonel Stewart. I can go back to the actual pagination numbering in the transcript, but this went on extensively, and we came back to it on numerous occasions. To say that this particular subject has not been thoroughly exhausted, I'm somewhat astonished. Nevertheless, my objection is simply we just can't repeat and rehash that which we have been doing for the past six weeks, and the position of the Prosecutors is that that's what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges have decided. You're going to give a list of documents that haven't been shown to the accused so that the registrar can prepare all those documents, all the documents that will be shown to the accused. The point has to be underlined to which you wish to draw the attention of the accused, the particular point that you wish the accused to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have already given the registrar a list of all the documents we need, and these documents have not been shown to the accused until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How many of them are there, please? How many?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: About 12 more documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, you have them?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. I have the list, but some of them have not been clearly specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wish us to proceed quickly, and it is important for the rights of the accused to be fully protected but also for us to be able to manage the time of this trial in the interest of the superior course of justice which the International Tribunal has to manage. I wish the Defence to very clearly indicate to the witness the point that they wish him to comment on. Let us begin straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The intention of the Defence was not to speak about the background of these events. We wanted to talk about the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question, General, is the following: Is this the complete document that you sent to three addresses, the three addresses mentioned here, or is something missing, and could you please explain this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this document is not complete because usually, as I would write reports about any meeting, I would always quote everything that was said at the meeting and everything that I had said at the meeting, and here on the first page of the document, I mentioned Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I suggest that you show on the ELMO the English text. I think that you will be able to manage. All right. Perhaps the English will do. Could you perhaps put the Croatian text there too so that the Judges could see technically how you wrote these reports from meetings with various persons? No, not both will do. Perhaps we can have them both together. They should be enlarged, and one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we please have it enlarged, focused, zoomed? Please show the Croatian text first, paper over paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you explain the technical way you did this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said here "Bob Stewart, Colonel," and then the main outline of what he said to me at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where do your own remarks start, what you said? What is the first sentence of what you said at that meeting, not Bob Stewart, but you? Where is your first sentence? Could you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first sentence I said is: "I believe that," Mr. President, "Mate Boban had to be in Vitez today."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just the context, why did you think he had to be in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is related to his making a statement concerning the crime in Ahmici and receiving support from top political leadership in terms of carrying out an investigation concerning Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you think is lacking in this document before this sentence? Could you show it exactly, exactly what is missing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, on the left-hand side, my own name and surname are missing or at least my name, and then saying what I said, again given an outline of what I said to Colonel Stewart. Also what is missing are these theses, that is to say, what I had discussed at that meeting with Colonel Stewart. In the previous document, this is even more obvious, I said, "Blaskic" and then everything else that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please show the previous document on the ELMO. Move it to the other side a bit so that we can see it exactly. Could you indicate this to us, where you mention the persons who are speaking and where you are quoting their words?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here, for example, "General Petkovic" and then everything that he spoke of, and then "Blaskic," my last name, and then everything that I spoke of. Then you can see further on "Sefer Halilovic" and everything that Sefer spoke of, and so on and so forth, "Mr. Thebault," "Petkovic," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please show us the first document that we were discussing? The second part of the text that are your own words and that begin with the following words show very unobjective information. Why did you make this suggestion to the head of the main staff in that sense?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the point was to get broader support, primarily public support in the area of the Lasva pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For carrying out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: An investigation about what?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: An investigation about the crime in Ahmici. It is a fact that there were crimes committed previously that were kept silent about and that the public was not informed about, and they were committed against Croats. It was very important to inform the public about those crimes too, so that in carrying out the investigation, I would have the full support of the public, notably, the people who lived in the Lasva pocket and the honest soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, General, you are saying that your words addressed to Colonel Stewart are missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you can ask the question to the particular witness as opposed to what he's saying, I think that would be more helpful and more spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I must ask the witness a question but I first have to make an introduction. The witness claims that his words have been left out, so my question was, "What has been left out?" But I have to make an introduction to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The introduction you are saying leads to a following of lines as to what the witness is saying. Let the witness say what the witness is going to say and not tell the witness what to say. That's a simple objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The witness has said many things in the last ten minutes, and in order to focus his attention to a particular point, I have to indicate that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Bear in mind the objection, and do not give the answer together with the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Certainly, I hadn't given the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking the General, what has been left out of this document, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that what I had said to Colonel Stewart had been left out, and that is that I had addressed the letter to him and that in that letter my answer is included and my position regarding the crime in Ahmici. I also told Colonel Stewart that Ahmici is within the area of responsibility of the HVO, and I also said that the HVO had not shelled Zenica because that too was a topic that we discussed on the 24th of April, 1993, as far as I can recollect. But, of course, to be sure of the details, I would have to look it up in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your part of your report, you mention the shelling of Zenica, but you don't mention that Stewart told you that. What can you infer from that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document is not correct in that respect because Stewart said to me that Zenica had been shelled, and I'm quite sure that I wrote that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But we are now disputing the document, if I understand very well, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The completeness of the document, because according to what the witness is claiming, a part of the document is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I must say that I regret that after six weeks - and this is my personal opinion - six weeks of debate, we wait for the last day to dispute a document and claim that there were different versions, but it's up to you. Mr. Kehoe, do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection is this: If we're talking about the document, that's one thing. Now we're talking about the Zenica shelling, and he's talking about this conversation that takes place on the 24th when the witness testified that his conversation with Stewart on the Zenica shelling took place on the 20th. So I'm a little confused. Are we just talking about this document, are we talking about the Zenica shelling, because that is what the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
